summary: Deep technical session on autoscaling and capacity planning for AstraMed's LLM workloads. Discussed queueing models, burst policies, reserved GPU sizing, batching and KV cache behavior, and VPC/on-prem constraints. Agreed to run benchmarks on customer traces and share a capacity planning spreadsheet and security docs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-22 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Rafael Ortega (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (AstraMed Head of ML), Jeff Lin (Platform Eng), Sara Gomez (Security)

Summary: quick recap at top: customer wants predictable p99 latency under 300ms for 7B and 1s for 13B with bursty traffic from web app; primary constraints are budget and SOC2 / VPC requirements.

[00:00] Maya (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, can we do quick intros? Rafael is our SE, he'll drive the technical parts.
[00:18] Priya (AstraMed): hi, Priya here, we own model infra and product ML, mostly concerned about latency and cost with spikes during morning syncs.
[00:27] Jeff (AstraMed): Jeff, platform eng, will own networking / VPC side, also curious about reserved capacity sizing.
[00:35] Sara (AstraMed): Sara from security, SOC2 and KMS questions.
[00:40] Rafael (Redwood SE): great, thanks. quick agenda: autoscale patterns, queueing model, burst policies, reserved GPUs, batching & kv cache behavior, and then open Qs about VPC/on-prem and quantization.

[01:02] Maya: just to note timeline — customer wants pilot in early November, so we need bench results and capacity plan this week.

[02:15] Rafael: start with a simple model of traffic — if you have steady baseline of X qps and spikes up to Y for short windows, autoscaling needs both headroom and fast ramp. two levers: reserved GPUs for baseline and burst pools for short spikes.

[03:10] Jeff: what counts as "short"? our spikes are like 1-3 minutes, not hours.
[03:18] Rafael: that matters. if spikes are under 5 minutes, it's often cheaper to use a burst pool and queueing rather than full scale-up because spin-up time for dedicated GPUs can be tens of seconds to a few minutes depending on provisioning.

[04:05] Priya: are we talking Redwood Dedicated, or something in our VPC? we need VPC/on-prem option for PHI.
[04:15] Rafael: yes, two deployment modes: Redwood Dedicated (reserved capacity in our infra) or Redwood Private deployed in your VPC/on-prem. for VPC we can pre-warm nodes in your account to reduce cold start. note: pre-warm increases committed cost.

[05:00] Sara: and KMS? keys must stay under our HSM.
[05:05] Rafael: we integrate with customer KMS/HSM. that doesn't affect scaling much, but we do need to configure key access and IAM up front — there will be a short handshake during instance boot for Private.

[06:12] Rafael: queueing model: two layers — front-end request queue (short TTL) and runtime scheduler which packs requests by length into batches. if queue fills, we can either increase concurrency per GPU or return 429/queue-depth backpressure.

[06:55] Jeff: how do you determine concurrency? we saw docs referring to K-V cache behavior that changes with concurrency.
[07:05] Rafael: good, the KV (sometimes transcribed as K-V) cache is per-worker and we keep KV warm between requests for the same session or prefix. high concurrency can evict the cache faster which increases tail latency for long-context flows. so there's a sweet spot: enough concurrency to improve throughput but not so high to trash KV.

[08:30] Priya: can we size reserved GPUs to keep KV hot for expected sessions?
[08:36] Rafael: yes, reserved capacity sized for baseline sessions keeps KV warm and gives stable p99. for spikes, we rely on burst pool but accept that new burst instances need to warm KV — that's where prefix caching and warmers help.

[09:10] Maya: note: pre-warm scripts exist, we can run synthetic warmers using your traffic traces to reduce warm penalty.

[10:20] Jeff: what about batching? latency-sensitive requests don't like big batches, but batching reduces cost.

[10:32] Rafael: we support dynamic batching with SLO-aware policies: set p50/p99 targets, the runtime will batch up to a max latency budget. for p99 under 300ms we keep batch windows small (1-10ms) and prefer concurrency scaling vs batch growth. for throughput jobs you can push larger batch windows.

[11:45] Priya: quantization — our team wants to use int8 or q4_0 to reduce memory on 13B. what's impact on latency/quality?

[11:55] Rafael: quantization helps memory footprint and can reduce latency slightly but may add CPU overhead for dequant/pack ops. 7B quantized to q4_0 often preserves perf and quality; 13B quantization helps fit onto fewer GPUs but test on your prompts — we'll include that in the bench.

[13:00] Jeff: reserved GPUs — how many to commit for baseline? any thumb rules?

[13:08] Rafael: rough rule: compute baseline RPS * median tokens-per-request * tokens-per-second throughput per GPU -> baseline GPUs. but because of sequence lengths variance, add 20-30% headroom. also consider KV warm factor for session-heavy loads. we'll provide a spreadsheet for this.

[14:20] Priya: can you walk through an example? say baseline 15 rps with average 60 tokens and spikes to 90 rps for 2 minutes.

[14:30] Rafael: sure — assume a given GPU yields 80k tokens/sec for 7B with our runtime at X batch/concurrency. baseline tokens/sec = 15 * 60 = 900 tps. that alone is ~0.01125 of a GPU, so baseline would be 1 GPU for redundancy and KV warm. add 20% headroom -> 1.2 ~ 2 GPUs if you want redundancy. for spikes to 90 rps -> 5400 tps short term, then you'd need 5400/80k = 0.0675 GPUs additional — seems small but real-world overheads, batching inefficiencies and latency SLOs push us to use burst pool of 1-2 GPUs. numbers are simplified; spreadsheet will calculate precisely.

[16:00] Sara: you said 80k tokens/sec — what's that measured on? hardware and model config?

[16:06] Rafael: measured on A100-like instances with optimized kernels and float16 execution on our runtime; quantization changes that number. for 13B it's lower, maybe 35-40k tokens/sec depending on ops. we'll include both model profiles in the bench.

[17:00] Maya: any concerns about rate limits and throttling from a product perspective?

[17:06] Rafael: yes, we enforce per-tenant rate limits and circuit-breakers. you can configure soft-queue with TTL and fallback behavior (retry, degrade to smaller model, or 429). common pattern: baseline reserved + burst pool + queue with preconfigured fallback to smaller quantized model when queue depth exceeds threshold.

[18:20] Jeff: how fast can burst pool spin up? we can't accept 3-5 minute cold starts for user-facing flows.

[18:28] Rafael: for Dedicated in Redwood infra, we can keep warm standby instances so spin-up is ~20-45s. in VPC/on-prem, if you pre-warm nodes or use pre-provisioning we can hit similar numbers; cold provisioning without pre-warm can be multiple minutes depending on cloud provider. tradeoff: standby nodes cost money.

[19:35] Priya: is there a hybrid option — reserved small footprint plus ephemeral GPU burst?

[19:42] Rafael: yes, hybrid is common: reserve minimal GPUs for baseline & KV warm, burst into cloud-backed ephemeral GPUs only when needed, use routing policies to move traffic. Redwood's smart routing can fallback to compatible model variants in different regions or capacity tiers.

[20:50] Sara: from security: when bursting to cloud, does data leave VPC?

[20:56] Rafael: depends on deployment: in Redwood Dedicated, data is kept in our infra with contractual protections. in Redwood Private deployed into your VPC, burst instances live in your VPC and data never leaves. if you use cross-account bursting we can encrypt in transit and ensure logs are forwarded to your SIEM, but you should review that with your security team.

[22:15] Jeff: queueing semantics — do you prioritize short requests?

[22:20] Rafael: we have priority queues and can implement latency-aware scheduling where small/short requests get higher priority to protect p99 for interactive flows. larger batchy requests can be deprioritized.

[24:00] Priya: can caching reduce load? we have many repeated prefixes.

[24:05] Rafael: yes, prefix caching + response caching can massively reduce compute. Redwood's cache can be local (per GPU) and global edge caches. if you have repeated prompts, cache hit rate can reduce required GPU count significantly. but caching works best for deterministic or near-deterministic prompts.

[25:40] Jeff: what about metrics and telemetry we get? we need token-level cost breakdown and p99 traces.

[25:46] Maya: Redwood Console provides per-route model breakdowns, tokens, latency histograms, and tracing hooks. we'll enable sampling at p99 and provide the dashboards.

[27:10] Rafael: one subtlety: KV cache eviction patterns show up as increased p99 correlated to session churn — we'll provide sample traces and visualizations. during bench we can replay sessionized traffic to measure this effect.

[29:00] Priya: on quantization again — for 13B is it worth moving to q4_0 or do we just scale GPUs?

[29:12] Rafael: often q4_0 is worth it to reduce memory and cost; you might accept a small quality delta. for regulated workloads you should test QA prompts. we'll run comparative evals in the bench.

[31:00] Jeff: do you support automatic fallback to smaller models during sustained high load?

[31:06] Rafael: yes, rollout/fallback policies allow canary, A/B, and automatic fallback to cheaper variants. you can configure triggers based on latency or error rate.

[33:00] Priya: how do we model budget impact of pre-warming standby instances?

[33:08] Rafael: spreadsheet will include uptime vs cost tradeoff. example: keeping one warm A100 costs X per hour, but avoids losing conversions if your burst causes degraded UX. often customers keep minimal standby for user-facing and rely on burst for less-critical flows.

[35:20] Sara: audit logs — will we get detailed request logs for SOC2?

[35:26] Rafael: yes, for Private we can forward audit logs to your S3 or SIEM; for Dedicated we provide audit exports and retention options. encryption-at-rest with your KMS is supported.

[36:40] Maya: quick pause — any blockers for doing the bench? we need access to sample traces and acceptance criteria for p99/p50.

[36:50] Priya: we'll share two days of production traces and a list of 20 QA prompts for regression testing.

[38:10] Rafael: good. bench plan: run both 7B and 13B (float16 and 4-bit quant), simulate baseline and spikes, run with reserved-only and hybrid reserved+burst config, measure p50/p90/p99, tokens/sec, KV hit-rate, and cost per 1k tokens.

[39:56] Jeff: what about model parallelism on 13B — do you recommend sharding vs more GPUs?

[40:05] Rafael: for 13B we typically fit the model on one GPU with quantization; otherwise we use minimal model parallelism. sharding adds latency due to cross-GPU comms. prefer quant or slightly larger instance to avoid cross-GPU sync if low latency is goal.

[41:40] Priya: can we run the bench in our VPC? we prefer not to share traces externally.

[41:47] Rafael: yes, we can run bench in your VPC using Redwood Private. we'll need temporary access to deploy bench orchestrator; we can run containerized workloads in your account and output metrics to your S3.

[43:00] Maya: any gotchas on networking — NAT, peering, or firewall rules?

[43:06] Jeff: we have strict egress controls.

[43:10] Rafael: for Private we need ports for orchestration, and image registry access or offline images for air-gapped. we'll send a network checklist.

[44:30] Priya: SLA expectations — how do you ensure p99 targets during region outages?

[44:36] Rafael: multi-region routing and fallbacks. you can set regional priorities and fallback policies to sister-region models. Dedicated customers can reserve across regions to match SLOs.

[46:00] Jeff: curious about cost-saving levers — aside from quant and batching?

[46:06] Rafael: prefix caching, response caching, model distillation/use of smaller models for some routes, and aggressive batching for background jobs. also use of reserved commitments for baseline gives big discounts.

[47:30] Priya: any standard burst policy configs you recommend?

[47:36] Rafael: yes, common: baseline reserve for 70-80% of expected median, burst pool sized for 95th percentile, and a short queue with 30-60s TTL and fallback to smaller model. that balances cost and UX.

[49:00] Sara: when bursting into public cloud with Private deployment, who's responsible for patching and security of instances?

[49:06] Rafael: if using Redwood Private deployed into your VPC, you control the instances and are responsible for host-level patching; Redwood provides the application container images and runtime patches. for Dedicated (Redwood-managed) we handle host patches and provide patch schedule.

[50:20] Jeff: any benchmarks from similar customers?

[50:26] Rafael: we ran similar pilots for a fintech customer, they hit p99 ~250ms for 7B with one reserved GPU + one warm standby and responsive burst pool. we'll share anonymized results.

[51:40] Priya: timeline recap?

[51:45] Maya: Redwood will: 1) run bench in VPC or isolated env on your traces, 2) share capacity spreadsheet and network checklist, 3) send SOC2/VPC/KMS docs. target deliverables by 2025-10-29; pilot kickoff week of 2025-11-03.

[53:10] Jeff: anything else we should consider for compliance?

[53:15] Sara: data retention policy and delete-on-demand.

[53:20] Rafael: supported — we'll configure retention and provide audit trails.

[55:00] Maya: ok if we wrap and capture action items?

[55:05] Priya: yep.

Action items (verbatim in transcript):
[55:30] Maya: Redwood action - send capacity planning spreadsheet and burst policy examples (Maya) - due 2025-10-24.
[55:45] Rafael: Redwood action - schedule bench, need traces and QA prompts (Rafael) - target run by 2025-10-27.
[56:00] Priya: Customer action - share two days of production traces and 20 QA prompts (Priya) - due 2025-10-24.
[56:20] Sara: Customer action - provide KMS / HSM contact and compliance checklist (Sara) - due 2025-10-24.

[57:00] Rafael: final notes — we'll simulate sessionized traffic to understand KV eviction and include warmers. expect a short follow-up with concrete numbers.
[58:10] Jeff: sounds good, thanks.
[58:20] Priya: thanks everyone, excited to see bench results.
[58:30] Maya: thanks all, we'll follow up with next steps and calendar invites.
[61:00] (call ends)
